blocks.text: A stack is a rule about which pending item is used next. It is not necessarily a special region of process memory, and it is not defined by whether its implementation uses an array or linked nodes. The last item accepted becomes the first item removed. That rule makes a stack a natural record of unfinished nested work.

blocks.text: This chapter connects the abstraction to two visible tasks: checking delimiters and evaluating postfix arithmetic. Both examples require a precise grammar and explicit failure behavior. Follow the contract all the way from input tokens to the final result.

Popping the observed element ends its lifetime in the sequence. Keeping a top reference across arbitrary mutations therefore requires care even when the interface does not expose iterators. Abstraction hides representation choices; it does not eliminate lifetime dependencies.

blocks.text: Review reasoning. Why can counts not prove delimiter nesting? They discard order. Why is a stack template not automatically strongly exception-safe for all types? Element moves and return construction can throw at different stages. Why check full token consumption? Prefix conversion is a weaker contract. Why is one remaining value required? A complete expression produces one combined result. Why does sequential correctness not imply thread safety? No operation establishes synchronization or an atomic multi-step observation.

reading.title: Guided lab — Build a diagnostic evaluator
paragraphs: Create a result type that distinguishes a numeric value from an evaluation error containing the token index and a category. Suggested categories are malformed integer, unsupported token, insufficient operands, result outside the supported domain, and unfinished expression. The categories are part of your exercise design; keep them stable enough that tests can assert them without matching an entire prose message.

Add division under a precise integer contract. Reject division by zero before evaluating it. State how negative division truncates in the selected C++ integer model and include examples with positive and negative operands. Keep the domain bounded so the exceptional minimum-integer divided by minus-one case is excluded, or explicitly handle it before arithmetic. Do not write a test that invokes undefined behavior and then asks whether an exception appeared.

For delimiter checking, return the position of the first impossible closing delimiter. At end-of-input, report that an opening remains unmatched. Decide which opening position to report when several remain; there is no single unavoidable policy. Store positions alongside opening types so the information exists when needed.

Generate short strings over the alphabet ()[] and compare your checker with an independent recursive parser for the same deliberately small grammar. A useful independent model parses a sequence of correctly nested groups, rather than duplicating the exact same stack algorithm with different names. Keep the domain small enough that enumeration terminates quickly.

Acceptance evidence. Include subtraction, empty input, extra operands, incomplete numeric tokens, nested mismatch, unmatched opening, unmatched closing, and both arithmetic boundaries. Preserve the input tokens on failure because the evaluator’s job is to compute, not rewrite the caller’s data.
